gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a typical 1,875 W US hair dryer needs 7.5× the TESSAN TC03's 250 W (9.4× the Ceptics 200 W). It also doesn't say that the only maker-listed pure-sine unit rated above that dryer is the Ceptics VC-S2000, at $129.99 for 2,000 W ($0.065/W, a 1.07× margin), against $0.176/W for the TC03.
standout_why: I compared against globalplugs.com/blog/voltage-converter-vs-adapter and voltwander.com/faq. Global Plugs gives a general rule ('A 1,500 W hair dryer needs a converter rated 2,000 W or more') and price bands ($30–150), but it names no product, gives no price per watt and has no 1,875 W case. VoltWander only says '2000W+' for dryers. ChatGPT's answer named the Ceptics 200 W and TESSAN 250 W units but never said how far short a US dryer falls. It also missed that some '2,000 W' combo units limit the 2,000 W outlet to mechanically controlled dryers, or have a 200 W port that does not convert at all. The manuals.plus PDFs and the Digital Camera World review would not render, so I could not check them.
decides: This confirms the TESSAN TC03 (250 W, $43.99) or Ceptics PU-200C (200 W, $34.99) for chargers, toothbrushes and shavers. For a 1,875 W US hair dryer, no compact 200–250 W combo works, so the pick moves to a 2,000 W unit. That means the Ceptics VC-S2000 (pure sine wave, $129.99), or the Ceptics LX-C2000 ($49.99) only if the dryer has mechanical switches. The VC-S2000 margin of 1.07× is thinner than Global Plugs' rule of about 1.33× (2,000 W for a 1,500 W dryer).
